$comment: R1736 — WHAT A PRESS ON THE ANALYSIS TOOL'S SCREENS GUARANTEES, written
down once, apart from the code that has to satisfy it.
WHY THIS IS A FILE AND NOT A RUST CONSTANT. The reason its siblings are.
A screen's own `spec` module is what a RUNNING screen needs — paint tags,
catalogue rows, the wording of a refusal — and a specification written
there is written by the same hand that has to satisfy it, so the gate ends
up asking the thing under test for the right answer (R1728). This file is
the other hand. It is tracked, it is read by the demo and by the screens'
own sweeps, and neither of them may edit it to pass.
WHAT OPENED IT. A person reported, on their own desktop, that a node
created from the palette could not be selected — and, decisively, that
'sometimes the node is selected and sometimes the background behind it is,
so dragging pans'. Every gate in the tree was green. Two things were true
at once and only one of them had been looked for:
1. a press was delivered to the screen one pixel left or up of where the
pointer actually was, at some coordinates and not others; and
2. the gate that watches 'the drawn thing is the pressed thing' sampled
ONE POINT per rectangle in the direction that convicts, and that point
was the middle.
Both are measured below rather than asserted. The vocabulary here is
neutral by requirement: this describes the analysis tool's screens, not any
particular product's.
THE PIXEL A POINTER IS AT IS THE PIXEL THE SCREEN IS TOLD ABOUT.
A screen that hit-tests itself is handed a FRACTION of its surface and
multiplies it back. The fraction was made by dividing an integer pixel
by an integer extent in 32-bit floating point, so the product lands a
hair either side of the pixel it came from — and truncating it turns 'a
hair below an integer' into the pixel before.
Measured by walking a real X pointer over 600 columns and 600 rows of a
running screen and asking it where it thought the pointer was:
35 of 600 columns and 20 of 600 rows arrived one pixel left or up.
After the repair, 0 and 0. This surface is that measurement kept.
It is stated per-pixel and not per-control on purpose. Which pixels fail
depends on the extent, so any list of points somebody chooses can miss
them all — which is exactly how this survived every gate.

canon.title: every column of the surface arrives as itself
every row of the surface arrives as itself

$comment: A CONTROL IS PRESSABLE OVER THE RECTANGLE IT WAS DRAWN IN, not only at
its middle.
The framework holds every tagged rectangle its last frame painted, so
this is askable as a total rather than sampled: each rectangle is probed
at nine points — its centre, its four edge midpoints and its four inset
corners — and every answer is judged against the paint. An answer naming
something else is sound exactly when the paint puts that something else
at that very point: a card's corner answering the pin that overhangs it
is the paint agreeing with itself, and the same corner answering the
canvas behind it is not.
Before R1736 the eight non-centre probes only ever RESCUED a rectangle —
they ran when the centre disagreed and could turn a defect into a grip.
A rectangle whose centre agreed was never asked anything else. Every
automatic observer in the tree aims at the middle, so the middle is the
one point that cannot convict.
THE FLOOR, MEASURED. A mature retained-mode toolkit was built and driven
for this: a canvas item that paints exactly the region it declares is
pickable at 100% of the pixels it was drawn in, under four camera
transforms including fractional zooms (13,500 / 9,450 / 11,718 / 9,919
points, no misses). That is a real floor and this tree owed it. What the
floor cannot do is notice when an author lets the two come apart: an item
whose paint reaches six pixels past its pick shape leaves 15.4% of its
painted pixels dead at zoom 100 and 84, and 30.1% at 135, while the
framework holds both rectangles, hands out the larger one as the item's
bounds, and never compares them. There is no verdict to read.

canon.title: the middle of the rectangle reaches what was drawn there
the four edge midpoints reach it or something drawn over it
the four inset corners reach it or something drawn over it
no point inside it resolves where the paint drew nothing

owed.sentence: nine points is a sample of a region, not the region
why: The honest statement is 'every point inside the rectangle', and nine
points is what a check can afford to ask of every painted rectangle
of every screen on every frame. The nine are chosen to be the ones a
transform error moves first — the middle is the last point to break,
which is why it was the wrong one to sample alone. A per-pixel sweep
is affordable for one control at a time and the demo does it for the
surface's own coordinate round trip, where the failures are dense.

$comment: THE DRAWN RECTANGLE AND THE PRESSED RECTANGLE ARE ONE RECTANGLE.
The invariant that makes the surface above unfalsifiable-by-drift rather
than merely watched. A screen is one escape hatch, so it hit-tests
itself; every such screen written here used to work out where it had
drawn something a SECOND time, from the model, and the two derivations
have parted four times in this repository's history — a doubled offset, a
pane-versus-window frame, an unscrolled pane, a stale window size. Each
was repaired on one screen and left the structure standing.
The framework painted those rectangles and still holds them, with the
names on them, so the press reads them instead. The priority among
overlapping marks is the paint's too: last drawn is topmost, which is
what the reader sees — the pin is over the card because the painter drew
it there, not because a hit test lists pins first.
This is not reachable from the floor's design. Measured on the same
6.11.1 build: of eight marks a self-painting widget drew inside itself,
the framework names ZERO, because the only record it keeps of a paint is
pixels and pixels carry no identity.

canon.title: a card is reached through the rectangle it was painted in
a pin is reached over its own paint, including where it overhangs
what is drawn on top is what a press reaches first

owed.sentence: the surface above measures layering on this screen now, not geometry
why: `whole_rectangle` is a COMPARISON of two answers — what a rectangle
addresses by name, and what a press inside it addresses — and it is
only a comparison while the screen derives the two separately. This
surface makes them one derivation, so on the families it covers the
census can no longer catch geometry drift; there is none to catch.
That is the better state and it is also a smaller claim, written
here so a later reader does not take a clean report for more than it
is. The screens that still hit-test from a model of their own are
where the original question still bites.

owed.sentence: a wire carries no tag of its own, so a press on one is still parsed from the model
why: A link is drawn as a stroke between two pins and the paint records no
named rectangle for it, so there is nothing in the store to resolve
against. Stated rather than hidden: it is the remaining half of this
axis on this screen, and closing it means giving a wire a painted
identity rather than teaching the hit test a second geometry.

owed.sentence: a host frame is still gripped by its strip through the model's rectangle
why: The frame's painted rectangle is the whole group, and a press over
its interior belongs to the card there rather than to the group — so
resolving the frame from its paint would make every card inside it
undraggable. The grip is the strip along its top, and the paint does
not name that strip apart from the box. Closing this means painting
the grip as its own named thing, which is a change to what the screen
draws and not only to how it is read.

$comment: A SELECTION MADE WITH THE POINTER REACHES THE PERSON, in the same
sentence as one made on the wire.
Measured three times: the wire's select said 'selected T-01' and a press
said nothing at all, because the sentence sat at the invoke site rather
than at the act. So the reader who uses the pointer heard nothing and the
agent who uses the wire heard everything — the wrong way round.
It matters most exactly where the surfaces above fail. A press that lands
on the wrong thing while the screen says nothing reads as 'I clicked and
nothing happened', which is the sentence the person who opened this file
used.

canon.title: a press that changes the selection says what is now selected
and the wire's own verb says the same sentence, once
a press that changes nothing says nothing
